lines.cap: Drop a hammer and a feather at the same moment, and the hammer wins easily.
But on the airless Moon, an Apollo astronaut tried it, and they hit the ground **together**.
So is it really the feather's lightness that holds it back? To find out, we need **forces**: the pushes and pulls behind every movement.
Let's balance forces, weigh things on the Moon, fight friction, time a journey, stretch a spring, and find out how forces turn and press.
A **force** is simply a **push** or a **pull**.
You can't see a force itself, but you can always see what it **does**.
A force can make something **start** moving, **speed up**, **slow down**, change **direction**, or change **shape**.
Remember those five as **S, S, S, D, S**: Start, Speed up, Slow down, Direction, Shape.
Forces are measured in **newtons**, written **N**, after the scientist **Isaac Newton**.
We measure them with a **newtonmeter**, also called a spring balance.
A small apple weighs about **1 N**, and a **1 kg** bag of sugar about **10 N**, here on Earth.
A force has a **size** and a **direction**, so we draw it as an **arrow**, pointing the way the force acts.
A **longer** arrow means a **bigger** force: a 10 N arrow is twice as long as a 5 N one.
Forces come in two families. **Contact forces** act only when objects touch: friction, air resistance, tension, and the normal force from a surface.
**Non-contact forces** act at a distance: **gravity**, **magnetism**, and **electrostatic** forces, from static electricity.
There are lots of named forces, but each one is still just a push or a pull.
**Weight** is the pull of **gravity** on an object. It acts straight **down**, towards the centre of the Earth, without touching.
**Friction** acts between surfaces that slide, or try to slide, past each other. It always **opposes** the motion.
**Air resistance**, or **drag**, is friction from a fluid, like air or water. It opposes motion too, and grows as you go faster.
**Upthrust** is the upward push from a liquid or gas. It's what makes things **float**: a floating swimmer's weight is balanced by upthrust.
**Tension** is the pulling force in a stretched rope, string, cable or spring.
The **normal force** is the support push from a surface, at **right angles** to it. A table pushes up on a book; the floor pushes up on your feet.
And two more non-contact forces: **magnetic** forces, between magnets and magnetic materials, and **electrostatic** forces, between electric charges.
So weight, magnetic and electrostatic forces are **non-contact**, while friction, drag, tension, upthrust and the normal force are **contact** forces.
Usually, several forces act on an object at once. To predict what happens, add them up, taking their directions into account.
The single overall force is called the **resultant force**.
**Balanced forces** are equal in size but opposite in direction, so they cancel out. The resultant force is **zero**.
With balanced forces, a still object **stays still**, and a moving object keeps moving at a **constant speed in a straight line**.
So you don't need an overall force to keep something moving, only to **change** its motion. A cruising car's driving force is exactly balanced by friction and drag.
**Unbalanced forces** don't cancel, so there's a resultant force, and it **changes the motion**.
Acting in the direction of motion, it **speeds the object up**; acting against the motion, it **slows it down**. It can also **change its direction**.
To find the resultant along a line, **add** forces acting the same way, and **subtract** forces acting the opposite way.
A **30 N** push against **12 N** of friction gives 30 − 12 = **18 N** forwards, so the box speeds up.
A skydiver shows it all. At first, their weight is bigger than the drag, so they **speed up**.
But drag grows with speed, until it **balances** their weight. Then they fall at a steady speed, called **terminal velocity**.
In everyday talk, **mass** and **weight** mean the same thing. In physics, they're different.
**Mass** is the **amount of matter** in an object. It's measured in **kilograms (kg)**, and it **never changes**, wherever you take it.
**Weight** is the **force of gravity** on that mass. It's a force, so it's measured in **newtons (N)**, and it changes if gravity changes.
Remember: **Mass is Matter**, in kilograms; **Weight is the Wrench** of gravity, in newtons.
**weight = mass × gravitational field strength**, or **W = m × g**. Think: **We Most Go**.
On Earth, **g** is about **10 N/kg**: more precisely, 9.8.
So a **2 kg** bag weighs 2 × 10 = **20 N**.
On the **Moon**, g is only about **1.6 N/kg**: about **one sixth** of Earth's, or six times weaker.
The bag still has a mass of **2 kg**, but it weighs only about **3.2 N**. That's why astronauts bounce around so easily.
And astronauts floating on the Space Station haven't lost their mass, or escaped gravity. They float because they're **falling** around the Earth, along with the station.
**Friction** acts between two touching surfaces that slide, or try to slide, past each other. It acts **opposite** to the motion, so it slows things down.
Zoom right in, and even smooth-looking surfaces are **rough**. Their tiny bumps catch on each other.
**Drag** is friction from a fluid: **air resistance** in air, **water resistance** in water. It gets **bigger the faster you go**, and the bigger the area pushing through.
Friction can be **useful**: it lets you **walk** without slipping, lets **tyres grip** the road, and makes **brakes** work.
And a **parachute** uses a huge area to make lots of drag, slowing a fall.
But friction can be a **nuisance** too: in machines, it **wastes energy as heat** and wears parts out, and drag slows cars and cyclists.
**Reduce** friction with **lubricants** like oil, or with wheels and rollers. Reduce drag by **streamlining**: a smooth, pointed shape the air flows past easily.
To **increase** friction, use rougher surfaces, like the **treads** on tyres, or the **studs** on football boots.
Now, the feather. It has a big area for its tiny weight, so on Earth, drag holds it back.
On the Moon, with no air, there's **no drag**. When the astronaut David Scott dropped the hammer and feather there in 1971, they landed **together**.
So without air resistance, **all objects fall at the same rate**. It's drag, not weight, that makes the difference.
**Speed** tells you how fast something moves: how far it goes in a certain time.
**speed = distance ÷ time**
With distance in **metres** and time in **seconds**, speed is in **metres per second (m/s)**. You'll also see kilometres per hour, and miles per hour.
A runner covers **100 m** in **20 s**. Their speed is 100 ÷ 20 = **5 m/s**.
Few journeys go at one steady speed, so we often use **average speed**: the **total distance ÷ total time**.
A car speeds up, slows down and stops at traffic lights, but its average speed sums up the whole trip.
A **distance-time graph** pictures a journey: time along the bottom, and distance up the side.
A **flat** line means the distance isn't changing: the object is **stationary**. It's not going backwards, just stopped.
A straight **sloping** line means a **steady speed**.
And the **steeper** the line, the **faster** the speed. In fact, the **gradient**, or steepness, **equals the speed**.
Remember: **Steeper is Speedier, Flat is Frozen**.
Pull on a spring, and it stretches. Let go, and it springs back.
The amount it gets longer is its **extension**: the **new length minus the original length**.
A **10 cm** spring stretched to **13 cm** has an extension of **3 cm**.
**Hooke's law** says that the **extension** of a spring is **proportional** to the **force** stretching it.
Proportional means **double the force, double the extension**. Treble the force, and the extension trebles.
So a graph of force against extension is a **straight line** through the origin.
But only up to the **elastic limit**. Below it, the spring is elastic: it goes back to its original length when you let go.
Stretch it **past the elastic limit**, and the line curves away. The spring is **permanently stretched**, and won't go back to its shape.
That's how a **newtonmeter** works: each newton stretches its spring by the same amount, so its scale has **evenly spaced** marks.
Make your own: hang a cup from a soft spring or a rubber band, add coins one at a time, and measure the stretch. Equal coins should add roughly equal stretches.
Forces can also make things **turn** around a **pivot**, like a door on its hinges, or a seesaw.
This turning effect is called a **moment**: **moment = force × distance from the pivot**.
The distance is measured from the pivot, at **right angles** to the force. Moments are measured in **newton metres (N m)**.
So a force turns more if it's **bigger**, or if it acts **further from the pivot**.
That's why a **long spanner** loosens a tight bolt more easily, and why door handles are placed far from the hinges.
Try it: push a door open near its hinges, then near the handle. Near the hinges, it's much harder!
**Levers**, like crowbars, seesaws and wheelbarrows, use this idea to make jobs easier.
A seesaw **balances** when the moments are equal: **force × distance** on one side equals **force × distance** on the other.
So a lighter child sitting further out can balance a heavier one near the middle: **300 N** at **2 m** balances **600 N** at **1 m**.
A bigger force doesn't always win: a small force far from the pivot can turn more than a big force close to it.
**Pressure** tells you how concentrated a force is on a surface.
**pressure = force ÷ area**
Force is in newtons and area in square metres, so pressure is in **newtons per square metre (N/m²)**, also called **pascals (Pa)**.
So **100 N** pressing on **2 m²** gives 100 ÷ 2 = **50 N/m²**.
The **same force** gives a **bigger pressure** on a **smaller area**, and a smaller pressure on a larger area.
That's why **sharp** knives, pins and nails work: a tiny area turns an ordinary force into a huge pressure, which cuts or pierces.
So a sharp knife doesn't cut better because you push harder. The same force on a smaller area gives a much higher pressure.
And it's why **wide** snowshoes, skis and tractor tyres stop you sinking: a large area spreads the force into a small pressure.
A camel weighs far more than a person, yet its wide, flat feet barely sink into soft sand, while a stiletto heel sinks into a lawn.
Try it, with an adult's help: one drawing pin pops a balloon with a gentle push, but spread the same push over lots of pins, and the balloon often survives.
Remember: **Moments multiply, Pressure pares down**: force × distance, but force ÷ area.

chapters.title: Recap: memory hooks and exam traps

lines.cap: Let's lock it all in.
**Start, Speed up, Slow down, Direction, Shape**: what a force can do.
**Mass is Matter**, in kilograms; **Weight is the Wrench** of gravity, in newtons. And **We Most Go**: W = m × g.
**Steeper is Speedier, Flat is Frozen**, on a distance-time graph.
**Moments multiply, Pressure pares down.**
Now, five exam traps to avoid.
One: mass is in **kilograms**, but weight is a force, in **newtons**.
Two: with **balanced** forces, a moving object keeps a **steady speed**. It doesn't need an overall forward force.
Three: friction and drag always **oppose** motion, and drag **grows** with speed.
Four: speed = distance **÷** time, and pressure = force **÷** area. Divide, don't multiply!
Five: a spring only obeys Hooke's law up to its **elastic limit**.
Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
What is the unit of force?
The **newton**, N.
A box slides at a steady speed in a straight line. What can you say about the forces on it?
They're **balanced**: the resultant force is **zero**.
A bag has a mass of 3 kg. What is its weight on Earth?
A cyclist rides 200 m in 25 s. What is their average speed?
Why does a sharp knife cut better than a blunt one?
Its tiny area gives a much **higher pressure** for the same force.
Brilliant work. Now try the Forces & Motion quiz in your Science Lab, to lock it in.
